results.reply: Ah, dear child, brew a tea of valerian root and a pinch of dried chamomile, sip it warm ere you retire, and lay a sprig of lavender by your pillow; the night’s visions will soon grow gentle. If the dreams still linger, a short walk at dusk, breathing the cool air, oft steadies the mind.

The Cailleach o’ the hill is the ancient hag who watches the stones by the fairy fort, a stern spirit who turns the winter snows and shapes the hills with her great staff. ’Tis said she roams the crags when the mist rolls in, and a humble offering of milk and a sprig of rowan may keep her from a harsh wind or a sudden chill. Beware to speak with respect, for she guards the old ways and the hidden paths of the hills.

A good draught of boiled water with a handful of fresh thyme and a spoon‑full of honey, taken three times a day, will ease the cough; if she can bear it, add a pinch of crushed mullein leaf to the brew. May the Good Lord watch over her swift recovery.

Aye, a stranger came down the road last evenin’, a tall man with a soot‑black coat and a curious accent. He lodged at the inn and asked about the herb‑gardens, but said naught else. If ye wish to know more, I can fetch what the inn‑keeper heard.

Aye, a wolf’s bite leaves fresh gnaw marks and a scent o’ fear; if the carcass is torn, gnawed clean and the wool scattered, ’tis likely the beast. Should you find only a single, clean cut and the rest untouched, consider a stray dog or a hungry fox, but no other creature I know of will take a whole sheep without leaving a trail. Take a look for footprints and tell me what you see, and we’ll set a proper hedge or charm to keep the rest safe.
